The team is eager to figure this out because we realize that there has to be an economic model for this network. Otherwise, we’re in the early bootstrap phase still and lots of people are getting excited to build on this. But it’s the number-one question for my team, from all the people building. “What’s that model going to be?” Everybody’s eager to figure this out and to do it in a way that we don’t fall into the traps of trying to create the incentives that we’ve seen in other networks, which just cause all kinds of unintended consequences. Looping back on the WordPress example, it can work really nicely. WordPress is a slightly different model because it’s a hosting model. But there are thousands and thousands of WordPress hosts out there that are doing just fine and it just works. You can host your site anywhere, you can move it anywhere. They compete to be the best host for your content, but it’s a very good model. As far as I can tell, it hasn’t created anybody to take all the market share or create these weird incentives where the product gets worse. There’s a very nice dividing line there between “I’m your host” and “you go and do whatever you want.” You can build an ad network if you want. You can build a store, you can build something else. Our business model doesn’t dictate what your business model should be, which is kind of what happens in these other networks when it’s only ads. “Oh yeah, come here, build your following on here and then we’re going to put ads on it. If you want to do anything else, no, no, no, it’s going to be ads.” Those are the kinds of things we think about. Talking about irreversible decisions, that’s going to be a huge one when we start to zero in on the right model to make sure that we can picture this scaling to billions of users and all kinds of businesses emerging on this network, not just one type that we happen to think about. You’ve mentioned Blacksky a handful of times in this conversation. I’ve been lucky enough to be at a dinner with Rudy [Fraser] who runs Blacksky. He’s prolific in talking about what it’s like to actually build on the ATmosphere and what a lot of the challenges have been. Because it hasn’t yet really, truly been decentralized. Now it’s my turn to say, I won’t go into the weeds of the protocol, but there are parts of the Bluesky stack and parts of the ATmosphere that have been pretty heavily centralized up until fairly recently. Is it easy to stand up a competitor, in the way that you’re describing people can stand up competitors to WordPress and operate in their own universe using the same tools and same access to end customers? Or is there still work to be done there? Because it hasn’t been easy up until now, at least using the example of Blacksky. Rudy deserves a lot of credit for taking those early risks when it was much harder to build and being the first to prove that it can be done, but it’s getting easier and easier. We are seeing more and more Bluesky- and Blacksky-style networks pop up pretty often. We’re actually seeing a whole bunch of energy in Europe. We’ve got Eurosky. W Social just launched. There’s another one I think that’s about to launch. It’s getting easier, and we’re investing a lot to make it as easy as possible. In addition to being an open protocol, all of Bluesky’s open source. You can take the Bluesky app and just fork it and go do your own Bluesky. That’s great, but we’re really also interested in people building other things that are microblogging on the network and making that super easy. We’re seeing Tangled as an example that a lot of people like to use recently because it’s a great project. They raised VC funding. It’s a social coding platform, like a social GitHub that’s growing really nicely using AT Proto for the social layer of the social coding aspect. Has nothing to do with microblogging, but it’s another thing that we can collaborate and integrate. People use both Tangled and Bluesky. It all just works together. But those are examples where it’s getting really easy to just build a new app on AT Proto and have it have social functionality. It doesn’t have to be an entire Bluesky-style network that you have to run. We put effort into making it easier. When Blacksky started two or three years ago, it was a big lift. You had to be very technical to do it. Now it’s gotten easier and easier. Finally, we haven’t talked about AI yet. AI makes it even easier. A lot of the growth we’re seeing now is that you can point to one of the AI coding tools on AT Proto and say, “Hey, build me a social app, build me a community.” And that makes it that much easier. Those are some of the tools and integrations that we’re working on on Jay’s new team, but that really changes the game pretty substantially for just how easy all this stuff is getting. I do have to ask you the AI question. You’re a software CEO again. How do software companies work in the age of AI? Have you rethought your teams? Do you have the traditional product-manager-designer-engineer trio? Or is everybody doing everything? It’s a small team and you’re the new CEO. So you have lots of opportunity to rethink everything. It is very empowering once you get it right. We have to use our exploration team as an example. That’s a three- to four-person team that’s launching at very high velocity, launching brand new products. It’s really fun when you have an existing company with existing resources and very senior talented people can then go after a new greenfield opportunity with these new tools. That’s when you see a ton of velocity. If you have an existing product with all the complexity of how it’s been built, AI helps, but you’re still dealing with that same complexity for a while. I see it accelerate everything in terms of the development pace. You still need great product managers, you need great designers. You need [to know] how to build. The building part is faster than what to build. The ideas are just as hard as ever, in a way harder because there’s so much noise out there and so many things popping up every day. Setting yourself apart, building something really great that lasts. Just because it’s faster with AI doesn’t make it any easier. We’ve talked a lot about standards and making AT Protocol and the ATmosphere a more standardized project at the IETF and whatever Swiss foundation is going to do name lookups. It feels like we’re going to recapitulate ICANN. But that’s a totally different episode of Decoder, and we’ll come to that drama when everything is successful. There is another standard that has already gone through all this. There’s ActivityPub. Mastodon runs an ActivityPub. Famously, Threads runs an ActivityPub, to whatever extent Threads runs on ActivityPub. There’s an argument that Meta did all of that just to satisfy European regulators, and that’s all it’s there for. Have you talked to the Threads team about integrating with ActivityPub or moving them to the ATmosphere? Once you become an official standard, I imagine that must be easier for them to continue throwing bones to European regulators. That would be the big unlock, right? That is the hundreds of millions of users on a nominally open network. Have they shown any interest? We have not talked to Threads. We’re definitely talking to Mastodon and ActivityPub. They definitely feel we’re very aligned. Our missions are very aligned. We’re all on Team Open together. These are two different standards that do slightly different things. And some use cases for ActivityPub are great and some are great for AT Proto. What are use cases that are good in ActivityPub and what are use cases that are better in AT Protocol? ActivityPub is based around this notion of a server. At the heart of it, you set up your own server, you control it, you run it, that’s your community, and then all the servers can federate if you want. You don’t have to, you can just run it by yourself, or you can plug into the federation, into the Fediverse. That’s how their system works. It works really well. They have a lot of successful governments who want to set up their own server infrastructure and run their own community infrastructure. AT Proto has a different goal. We don’t have a server at the heart of it. We have the PDS, the personal data server that is your data. The heart of AT Proto is personal identity and portability and ownership of that so that whatever you create and the social graph that you create is owned by you and lifts wherever you want to host it. It’s really a federation of millions and millions of these tiny little personal servers that can all talk to each other. That works if your social product is focused on people, not on an entire server with a community on it. So a slightly different shape. They interoperate too. There’s something called Bridgy Fed that connects these two worlds together. So if you’ve built products on this yourself, if you want to post or publish across all of it, you can and the end user doesn’t even have to know. That’s the beauty of an open protocol: you shouldn’t have to. Consumers of this should never even hear about these new protocols. Because it’s one of these things where you have to get the protocol right and it has to be open, but then people should just forget about it. It should just disappear. The examples we use a lot are email and websites. If I’m on Outlook and you’re on Gmail, we can just email each other. You never think about the fact that those are two completely separate systems. It just works. But on social media, it just doesn’t work that way. If you’re on Instagram and I’m on TikTok, we can’t talk to each other. You have to do everything five different times and on five different apps, and it’s crazy making. If we get this right at the protocol level, that just goes away. All this stuff just works just like email does or just like websites do. Our job is to make all of that work under the hood, but nobody has to think about it. In the end, you just have one account, you log in anywhere and it just works, and all your friends are there and all your data’s there. And you never have to be locked in again into somebody’s system [where] you can’t leave. This is very nice, but it’s rare that two standards that nominally seek to achieve the same thing coexist forever. There are not two Bluetooths, there are not two Wi-Fis. There are not even two webs. People can argue with me about how many webs there are, but there are not even two webs. Do you expect ActivityPub and AT Protocol to coexist? Do you expect, I don’t know, Bluesky to be able to show content from Mastodon servers and then slowly eat ActivityPub as a protocol? That’s one very common pattern that happens in these situations. Or do you expect long-term coexistence? I expect long-term coexistence because both of these protocols have enough users and use cases that want to continue on. They can talk to each other when you want, but that’s not the main use of it. There are a lot of people who run ActivityPub instances who don’t even want to talk to other Mastodon servers. They just want to run their own thing. They don’t want to talk to AT Proto, but they can if they want. I don’t know what a good example is from other platforms. But they’re both going to be around for a long time and they’re just slightly different tools. They’re both in the social space, but they’re different tools that you reach to for different types of use cases. I’ll put it this way: In my mind, both can be wildly successful, and it’s not one or the other. AT Proto doesn’t need to eat ActivityPub to be successful, or vice versa. We’ve already seen that. I want to end by talking about the consumer app a little bit more. We’ve talked a lot about the protocol, the ATmosphere, the standards. We’ve gotten all the way to the internet engineering task force in this conversation. We’ve been in the weeds of how the technology works and how it’s governed. And right next to that is, well, it’s an election year here in the United States. And a lot of people truly believe that Bluesky is the wild progressive social media network and it is a bubble of one kind. X is a very different kind of bubble. It’s the hard-right network that has vastly more AI-generated anime porn on it. There’s not some thing that is actually the global town square. That thing has maybe gone away and all the social networks have fragmented. Do you want Bluesky to have the reputation it has? Do you want it to get bigger? Do you think that the right answer is someone starts a MAGA Bluesky and it interoperates the way that it needs to? This is the perception of the consumer product. Do you want that to change, and how would you change it? Yes, we definitely want that to change. It is already changing. It certainly wasn’t designed to attract one specific group of people. It works for anyone. What we see is there is a lot of political discourse on Bluesky and any of these open networks. People are very engaged. What we’ve seen in the lead up to the election so far – we’ve hosted a lot of live election feeds, and we see a lot of really good feedback from our users, a lot of engagement, a lot of, “This is actually really interesting content about this topic.” Whereas on other platforms, I think these election topics just get completely overwhelmed by slop and spam. It’s just noise and chaos. What we’re focusing on is to deliver a live experience. We do it around elections. We do it around sports as well, very successfully, where the people on the network that participate get a really good experience and get really good content. Once we have that, then hopefully we can just keep expanding to more and more types of users and use cases. We’re an open network for anyone and we don’t want to serve just one type of user base. I’ve seen it already in the last few months, really trend in the right direction where we just have more and more people show up and build their own corners of the network. It sort of balances out over time. We don’t just have a few topics you’re super deep on, but it just gets more and more diverse. In my opinion, yes, it’s a public square, but we don’t need everybody talking at the same time. Policy is very loaded, but if you’re super into sports, you’re not going to be into all sports. I’m super into the San Francisco Giants, so that’s what I want to follow. I don’t need to follow all of sports, and that’s fine. It can be like that with all topics. It just needs to be civil and positive and we need to have the tools that if it goes off the rails, people can regulate it and can have a good experience instead of it just devolving into a shouting match. By “people can regulate it,” you mean people can moderate their own feeds, not regulators can moderate speech? 100%, yes. Just checking. That’s important. Build their own feeds, pick their own feeds. We have very good tools for people to mute and block. We spend a lot of energy on making sure it stays positive because again, we’re interested in social media that actually serves the common or the public good. That’s not going to work if it’s just people yelling. You’ve talked a lot about the network. Even in this answer, I said Bluesky the app has this reputation, and you started talking about the network. It’s true, the network can serve everybody. Anybody can start whatever kind of app on the ATmosphere they want and they can go target the users they want. But I want to push you again on Bluesky the app. The thing that has a brand that exists out in the world that is totally divorced from the technical specifications of the ATmosphere. There is Bluesky the app and it does have a reputation. Do you want more users from X to leave X and join Bluesky and expand what that brand is for people? Yes. It can stay on X too. You don’t have to pick one or the other, but yes. Have you talked to Elon about federating X? I suspect he’s not interested. No, same answer with Threads. It would be full circle, right? Bluesky started inside Twitter, and then Twitter went away and became X. And then if X adopted AT Proto, then the whole original idea of the project would actually come to fruition. Yeah. This is Jack Dorsey saying Twitter wants to be AT Protocol, not a product. Here we are, and that’s Bluesky in big ways, but it is also a product. People know what that logo means. Political pundits say “the Bluesky crowd,” and that signifies whatever they want it to signify. I’m just wondering if you want to break that branding in any meaningful way. Yeah, we want to expand it. “Breaking” is maybe the wrong word, but yes, we want to expand more and more so that Bluesky means not just one thing, not just liberal politics, for example. I will point to sports as an example from the last year. We’ve made a very concerted effort to bring on sports leagues and sports writers, and it’s worked really well. There are a ton of sports conversations now on the app, and those people come here for the sports, not for the liberal politics. It’s possible to expand. In politics, it’s probably our hardest challenge because we have one type of user base there that’s very active. That’s good too. They are super active, and they’re very much at the forefront of politics and very engaged and very informed. But we can just keep adding more communities so that it balances out. It feels like we’re going to have to have you back, particularly as these private communities launch, to talk about where things go from here. But this has been great. Thank you so much for being on Decoder. Thank you very much for having me. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

articles.title: Science funding cuts will harm Britain’s global standing | Letters
articles.snippet: Readers respond to an editorial about the threat to research funding, including plans to close the Jodrell Bank Observatory Your editorial rightly criticises the decision to cease funding the Lovell telescope from March 2028 (The Guardian view on the Lovell telescope: budget cuts to physics are bad science and worse politics, 31 July). There are additional reasons why this decision is so shortsighted. Modern astronomy is no longer simply physics. It brings together physics, chemistry, biology and computing to understand how the universe evolved and where we came from. The universe is an inexpensive laboratory in which we can study the interaction of physical, chemical and biological processes under conditions that can never be reproduced on Earth. Understanding how galaxies formed and evolved requires complementary observations across the radio, optical and infrared spectrum. The whole is greater than the sum of its parts. As a PhD researcher at Jodrell Bank in the 1960s, I saw first-hand how its innovations transformed radio astronomy. Jodrell played a pioneering role in the development of long-baseline radio interferometry, which links separate telescopes together to create virtual telescopes thousands of miles across. Removing the Lovell telescope from this network would weaken its ability to produce pictures of the radio universe with a sharpness comparable to that achieved by billion-pound space observatories such as Hubble.
